title: RSU Diversification: How to Reduce Employer-Stock Risk
summary: At 40% employer-stock concentration, a 30% fall cuts your portfolio by 12%. Compare RSU sale paths, Indian tax and trading-window restrictions.
body_markdown:
Reduce employer-stock exposure by measuring your owned shares, comparing after-tax sale paths within permitted trading windows, and choosing where to reinvest. At 40% employer-stock concentration, a 30% share-price fall cuts your portfolio by 12%, even when everything else stays unchanged.


This applies when vested RSUs have become a meaningful part of your investible wealth. Your tax position and trading windows affect how quickly you can sell. Future grants and overlapping funds affect how much exposure remains.


## What is RSU diversification, and why does employer concentration matter?


RSU diversification means reducing how much of your wealth depends on your employer, then deciding where the proceeds belong. Concentration risk arises when a large part of your portfolio is tied to one asset, such as your employer's stock. RSUs can grow into a significant part of your wealth over time.


Your salary and investments can depend on the same employer. A business setback can therefore affect your income just as your largest investment falls.


Diversification spreads investment exposure across companies and other assets. As[FINRA's concentration-risk guidance](https://syndication.finra.org/content/concentrate-concentration-risk-0) explains, apparently different holdings can still share underlying risks.


If you are choosing between holding, selling and moving shares, start with the broader[vested-RSU decision framework](https://paasa.com/blog/what-to-do-with-vested-rsus-india) . Compare how much employer exposure you retain under each choice.


## How much of my portfolio is actually tied to my employer?


Calculate employer-stock concentration by dividing the current value of your owned employer shares by total investible assets.


Include those shares in the denominator, alongside other investments and investment cash. Exclude your primary home, future salary and unvested grants. Keep an emergency reserve outside this denominator if it is unavailable for investment, and use that convention consistently.


Track future grants separately by vest date: they are conditional awards rather than owned shares. Record salary and expected bonuses alongside the worksheet as employment exposure, rather than adding them to investment wealth.


Then look through your funds. Suppose you own ₹12 lakh of employer shares and a ₹10 lakh fund with a 5% holding in your employer. Your look-through company exposure is ₹12.5 lakh: ₹12 lakh + ₹0.5 lakh through the fund.


Sector overlap needs a second check. A technology fund can duplicate your employer's business risks even when it holds little of that particular stock. Compare underlying holdings, sectors and countries, rather than counting fund names.


## What would an employer-stock fall do to my overall wealth?


Suppose you hold 200 vested employer shares worth $100 each on 20 November 2026. Your total investible portfolio is $50,000, including these $20,000 of shares.


Assume ₹86 to the dollar for the current valuation and sale estimate. Your portfolio is worth ₹43 lakh, with ₹17.2 lakh in employer shares.


This stress test compares the existing position with a hypothetical reduction to 10%, before sale tax, on the same valuation date. Other holdings and the exchange rate stay unchanged during the assumed fall.


Measure Before reducing exposure After reducing exposure


Total portfolio ₹43 lakh ₹43 lakh


Employer shares ₹17.2 lakh ₹4.3 lakh


Employer-stock weight 40% 10%


Loss after a 30% employer-stock fall ₹5.16 lakh ₹1.29 lakh


Total portfolio decline 12% 3%


The arithmetic is ₹17,20,000 × 30% = ₹5,16,000, compared with ₹4,30,000 × 30% = ₹1,29,000.


Result: the same company shock costs ₹3.87 lakh less in the lower-exposure scenario, before sale tax.


The 10% figure is an illustration. Choose your own exposure limit by testing whether the loss would disrupt a financial goal.


## What changes if I sell now, sell gradually or redirect new investments?


RSU diversification strategies differ mainly in speed and how long you remain exposed. Selling all at once removes the single-stock position fastest. Staged sales spread your exit across different prices, while new investments dilute the position without selling it.


This comparison shows how the three approaches work on the example's valuation date.


Approach Exposure reduced Tax due Time still exposed Trading restrictions


Sell the chosen amount now Immediately on execution Gain on that sale Remaining shares stay exposed Current window and clearance apply


Sell in stages After each completed sale Separate gain or loss per tranche Until the final planned sale Each sale needs a permitted route


Redirect new investments Weight falls as other assets grow Existing shares remain unrealised Potentially years New employer-share sales still need permission


In the example, retaining ₹17.2 lakh of employer shares while diluting their weight to 10% requires a ₹1.72 crore portfolio. With prices unchanged, that means adding ₹1.29 crore elsewhere. Redirecting savings can therefore be slow when the existing position is large.


Staged sales can accommodate different holding periods, but future prices and currency rates change each tranche's result. Use the[RSU selling framework](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-sell-rsus) to compare the trade-offs, rather than assuming gradual selling always costs less tax.


## How do the 24-month holding period and 12.5% rate apply to my foreign-listed RSU shares in India?


For sales in tax year 2026-27, the[Income-tax Act, 2025, as amended](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/income_tax_act_2025_as_amended_by_fa_act_2026-pdf) distinguishes these holdings by their acquisition-to-sale period. For ordinary RSU shares, use the vesting/acquisition date recorded for the lot.


The answer to “India foreign listed shares capital gains tax 24 months 12.5% 2025 vested RSU employer” is this holding-period split:


Holding period Classification Indian tax on the gain


24 months or less Short-term capital gain Your applicable slab rate


More than 24 months Long-term capital gain 12.5%, without indexation


Applicable surcharge and cess are additional. The tax applies to the capital gain, rather than the full sale proceeds.


The[RSU capital-gains guide](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) explains the distinction in more detail. Waiting for long-term treatment leaves the shares exposed during the waiting period, so compare the potential tax saving with the loss your portfolio could absorb.


## How do I use my shares’ vesting value to calculate their cost and capital gain?


Vesting creates salary income through the taxable perquisite. A later sale creates a separate capital gain or loss.


For “India foreign RSU shares capital gains 24 months 12.5% vesting fair market value cost tax”, start with the value already used for that perquisite. Section 73(1) of the Act carries that fair market value into acquisition cost.


Continue the example. Suppose the retained shares vested on 15 September 2023 at $80 each, with a payroll conversion rate of ₹82 to the dollar. You sell 150 shares on 20 November 2026, after more than 38 months.


For this planning estimate, translate gross sale proceeds at the current rate above and subtract the recorded INR perquisite basis. Assume no deductible sale charges.


1. Calculate the basis: 150 × $80 × ₹82 = ₹9,84,000.
2. Calculate sale proceeds: 150 × $100 × ₹86 = ₹12,90,000.
3. Calculate the gain: ₹12,90,000 − ₹9,84,000 = ₹3,06,000.
4. Calculate base long-term tax: ₹3,06,000 × 12.5% = ₹38,250.
5. Recalculate concentration after reserving that tax: ₹4,30,000 ÷ (₹43,00,000 − ₹38,250) × 100 = approximately 10.09%.


Result: selling 150 shares reduces employer exposure from 40% to approximately 10.09%, after base tax but before cess or surcharge.


Currency movement is included: the INR gain reflects both the share-price change and the different conversion rates. The applicable return-conversion treatment needs lot-specific tax review.


For “India foreign RSU shares capital gains tax cost basis fair market value vesting perquisite double taxation schedule FA”, keep the payroll and investment records together. Gather vest confirmations, the perquisite valuation, Form 16, withheld-share details and sale confirmations, including fees and exchange-rate evidence. The[RSU tax-calculation guide](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-calculate-rsu-taxes-india) provides the wider calculation workflow.


## How do trading windows and other restrictions affect when I can sell?


Your employer's policy determines the trading calendar and any pre-clearance requirement. Released shares, lock-ups and transfer restrictions also affect execution. Build these into your[RSU selling rule](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-build-an-rsu-selling-rule) , including what happens when a planned sale falls inside a blackout.


For “RSU vested shares transfer brokerage blackout period sell trading window 10b5-1 diversification”, start with that policy. Moving custody preserves your exposure to the same shares; sale permission remains a separate question.


For “SEC employee insider trading blackout 10b5-1 plan material nonpublic information cooling off”, the[SEC's Rule 10b5-1 guidance](https://www.sec.gov/resources-small-businesses/small-business-compliance-guides/insider-trading-arrangements-and-related-disclosures) explains qualifying pre-arranged plans and cooling-off conditions. Some employers permit these plans; eligibility and approval are employer-specific.


If custody is the obstacle, use the relevant broker workflow, such as[moving Morgan Stanley shares or cash](https://paasa.com/blog/transfer-rsu-proceeds-from-morgan-stanley-to-paasa) . Keep that operational choice separate from the amount of employer stock you want to retain.


## Could my employer shares also affect my estate-tax exposure?


Yes. Shares of US-incorporated companies are generally US-situs assets, wherever your broker holds them. The[IRS's nonresident estate guidance](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/some-nonresidents-with-us-assets-must-file-estate-tax-returns) identifies a $60,000 US-situs filing threshold for estates of nonresident non-citizens; applicable estate-tax rates can reach 40%.


For estate tax, US domicile is distinct from income-tax residence. The[Form 706-NA instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i706na) explain the domicile test. Citizenship and treaty provisions also affect the result; location or visa status alone gives only part of the picture.


Diversification, Indian capital-gains tax and estate-tax situs are three separate checks. Moving the same stock to another broker preserves its situs. Replacing it with a US-domiciled ETF can broaden company exposure while retaining US-situs exposure.


Use the[US estate-tax guide](https://paasa.com/blog/how-us-estate-tax-works-for-indians-and-nris) for the rules and the[estate-tax calculator](https://paasa.com/tools/us-estate-inheritance-tax-calculator) for an illustrative estimate based on your circumstances.


## Where can I reinvest the proceeds without duplicating my existing risks?


Selling your employer's stock reduces the position. Where you reinvest determines the exposure you hold afterwards.


If you are working out how to diversify investments after receiving rsus, compare each destination against what you already own. A broad equity fund may still hold your employer. A technology fund may retain much of the same sector exposure.


Choose the destination's role first: long-term equity growth, a different regional allocation or lower-volatility assets for a nearer goal. Then examine its underlying holdings and domicile separately.


You can also assess[reinvesting RSU proceeds without bringing them back to India](https://paasa.com/blog/diversify-rsus-without-bringing-money-back-to-india) . That guide covers the money route and its conditions, so the custody decision can follow your allocation decision.

## When should I diversify?


Start reviewing when a plausible employer-stock fall would disrupt a goal. Revisit the calculation whenever new RSUs vest, as your exposure can gradually increase over time.


1. Inventory owned shares and other investible assets using one valuation date.
2. List future grants separately and check fund holdings for overlap.
3. Stress-test a company-specific fall against your financial goals.
4. Collect payroll and lot records, then compare the after-tax sale paths.
5. Check release status, trading windows and any clearance requirement.
6. Choose the proceeds' destination and review its underlying exposure and situs.
